audience.programmeDescription: International Development Studies examines inequality, poverty, livelihoods, food systems and environmental change through sociology, economics, communication, law and governance. This Dutch-taught bachelor combines a common foundation with a specialisation, field research and a thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR programme combines social theory, political economy, farming and environmental governance. The alternatives give greater weight to economic models and evidence, or to culture, social power and communication. WUR retains a more concentrated rural-development and field-research sequence.

curriculum.limitation: This 180-credit example contains 114 common credits, 24 taught specialisation credits, a 12-credit thesis and 30 open credits. General and fieldwork safety are additional zero-credit requirements. All prescribed taught study is completed before the thesis.

componentNotes.bin-field-methods: Fieldwork safety is mandatory. Research design, problem analysis and rural-livelihoods study prepare the qualitative and quantitative field-research training.
componentNotes.bin-field-practical: Required field research in the Netherlands, England or Ireland: proposal preparation, two weeks of individual fieldwork, then analysis and reporting. Complete fieldwork safety and prepare through the field-methods course.
componentNotes.bin-rural-sociology: Complete fieldwork safety. Prior social and development theory and study of agricultural development, political sociology and food globalisation prepare the course.
componentNotes.bin-thesis: Required 12-credit supervised literature-based research project; empirical research may supplement it. Entry requires at least 102 prescribed credits including all first-year courses, plus at least two of the four named specialisation courses. This example completes all prescribed taught courses before the thesis.
componentNotes.bin-electives: Thirty open credits for a minor and/or individual electives at WUR or another university. No particular package or exchange is required.
componentNotes.bin-academic-skills: Academic, research and personal development skills and career reflection. General safety is an additional zero-credit requirement.

concepts: Examines how inequality, institutions and environmental change shape livelihoods through sociology, economics, policy analysis, colonial and Indigenous histories, farming and mixed research methods.

Prioritises economic explanations of distribution and policy: microeconomics, macroeconomics, public and behavioural economics, econometrics and mathematical methods, applied alongside farming, environmental governance and qualitative inquiry.

Investigates power and social change through sociology, colonial and Indigenous histories, environmental justice, African heritage, media and public communication, supported by qualitative research and statistical foundations.

notes.text: WUR provides a dedicated sequence in development theory, rural households, agrarian change, food systems and supervised field research. UCR offers substantial responses through social theory, economics, farming, environmental governance and communication, while specialist rural-livelihoods theory, integrated development fieldwork and the required thesis remain differences.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Governance of Sustainability
selectedCourseDescriptions.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
